video_title: Making Sense of the Midterms - with More Perfect Union's Faiz Shakir
gist: Hasan Minhaj opens with a monologue arguing Trump's three 2016 promises (immigration, shaking up Washington, making voters richer) have failed on the third, with tariffs, ACA subsidy repeal and Iran-war gas prices driving a midterm backlash and an affordability message for Democrats; he then interviews Faiz Shakir (Bernie Sanders adviser, More Perfect Union co-founder) on oligarchy-as-affordability, the California billionaire tax, Medicare for All, AIPAC spending ($43M against one Michigan Senate candidate), AOC and 2028. Pure politics, no market content beyond gas prices, tariffs and wealth-tax/billionaire-flight claims; several ad reads are skipped.

insights.claim: Minhaj argues Trump's political pact rested on three promises (tough immigration, shaking up Washington, making voters richer); immigration is the one where he lost least support because border crossings are reportedly down over 80% from pre-inauguration levels and ICE arrests are up, while the economy promise is the one failing.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Immigration is a relative GOP strength; the midterm damage is economic.

insights.claim: Republican confidence in Trump's economic decisions reportedly fell from 92% at his November 2024 election to 67% two years later, and 60% of registered voters say his policies made the economy worse.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Erosion inside the GOP base on the economy is the key midterm risk indicator.

insights.claim: Tariffs are reported to cost the average US household about $1,000 a year, and repeal of Obamacare subsidies pushed premiums up enough that millions lost insurance; Minhaj frames these as policies directly traceable to Trump's own decisions.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Policy-attributable cost increases are harder for incumbents to deflect than exogenous inflation.

insights.claim: The Iran war is cast as Trump's most damaging decision because it spiked gas prices, 'the most important number in American politics'; Trump compounded this by taking ownership ('a very inexpensive price to pay') instead of blaming oil-market variables.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Energy-price spikes from the Iran conflict translate straight into approval losses; oil is a political variable.

insights.claim: Shakir says gas prices are the most visible daily price signal and a symbol of economic strain, but not the biggest budget item; he points to healthcare premiums, home and car loans, college and child care as the larger, 'rectifiable' structural costs a median family faces.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Progressive affordability platform targets big-ticket household costs rather than headline prices.
insights.quote: it is a a um good symbol of a lot of the problems in the economy

insights.claim: Shakir argues affordability is a symptom of concentrated economic power: when airlines and other industries carve up regions and collude, consumers lose the ability to shop around and have no recourse on price or quality.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Antitrust and consolidation become the causal story behind cost-of-living politics.
insights.quote: affordability is just a symptom of the fact that huge economic actors have colluded to raise the price on you

insights.claim: Minhaj says the most effective Democratic message in this cycle and into 2028 is that Trump and Republicans are making life more expensive, crediting Zohran Mamdani for handing the party the affordability playbook.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Expect Democrats to converge on cost-of-living messaging across the 2026-2028 cycles.

insights.claim: Shakir says the California billionaire-tax ballot proposition may fail because heavy spending (he claims 99%) warns it will bankrupt the state; he attributes this to novelty and fear-mongering and says passage would require voter boldness akin to electing a Medicare for All president.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Outcome is a read on whether wealth taxes can survive concentrated opposition spending.

insights.claim: Shakir rebuts the billionaires-will-leave argument by pointing to Florida, which gained billionaires yet is cutting education funding, arguing an influx of billionaires does not improve average residents' lives.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Challenges the tax-competition premise behind opposition to state wealth taxes.

insights.claim: Shakir speculates billionaires want low-tax jurisdictions to build data centers and live, citing Trump-led delegations to Saudi Arabia, Dubai and Qatar before the Iran war, and says their bottom line is who taxes them least and lets them rule.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: If tax regimes tighten, expect capital and data-center siting to shift to Gulf jurisdictions.

insights.claim: A poll cited by Minhaj found 66% of Republicans call the rich-poor gap a 'big problem', and Shakir agrees many MAGA voters are 'Bernie curious' but doubt whether government can function at scale.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Populist economic ideas have cross-party resonance; execution credibility is the barrier.

insights.claim: Shakir contends the media habitually treats 'too far left' as the danger, never 'too far right', because redistribution toward the bottom 60% threatens the top 5% for whom, he says, there has never been a better time; he argues massive wealth has transferred to the top 1% over a long period.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Framing of policy risk is itself shaped by who benefits from the status quo.

insights.claim: Shakir says winning outside the two-party system is nearly impossible without billions for ballot access, so progressives must win Democratic primaries; this cycle produced the most progressive-populist primary wins, but also losses.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: The progressive path to 2028 runs through the nomination, not a third party.

insights.claim: Shakir identifies the central obstacle for a progressive presidential nominee as Democratic primary voters' electability concern: they are 'curious and interested' but worry a populist could scare off general-election voters.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Electability perception, not ideology alone, gates progressive nominations.

insights.claim: Shakir hopes AOC runs in 2028 and wants a crowded field of candidates running on Bernie-style vision; he says donors would prefer 'anyone but Bernie, anyone but AOC'.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Donor-class resistance is expected to shape the 2028 field and money flows.

insights.claim: Shakir says the progressive movement now has more institutional structure than in 2015-16, but any national candidate needs a large strategic operation to face huge establishment spending, plus must reach undecided voters rather than rooms of 50 existing fans.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Operational infrastructure is the differentiator versus Sanders' earlier runs.

insights.claim: Shakir says the Democratic leadership's problem is cowardice and aversion to hard structural fights (lowering Medicare age from 65 to 55 and the like), contrasting it with the GOP outsourcing everything to a strongman president.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Predicts continued intra-party friction between structural reformers and cautious leaders.
insights.quote: There's incredible amount of cowardice in the political system

insights.claim: Shakir says Mamdani-style local governance shows bold progressive policy can work, but that national success requires a president who attacks government dysfunction daily and changes how agencies like HHS operate.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Governing competence is the credibility gap for left-populism.

insights.claim: Shakir says AIPAC spent $33 million against Abdul in the Michigan Democratic Senate primary and is adding $10 million in the general election, about $43 million, notably backing Republican Mike Rogers for a seat Gary Peters holds; he says it is the only general-election spending AIPAC is doing.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Sets a benchmark for single-issue lobby spending and a test of whether it backfires.

insights.claim: Shakir argues AIPAC ads avoid discussing Israel at all and instead smear candidates, which breeds anger and, he says, ferments hostility toward Israel; he thinks 2028 Democratic hopefuls will be judged on whether opposition to military aid is sincere or scripted.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Opposition to Israel military aid is becoming a Democratic primary position, not a fringe one.

insights.claim: Shakir claims the Democratic base's anger is partly that party leaders privately know supporting Netanyahu is wrong yet cannot find their voice; he says Sanders pushed behind the scenes for Gaza to be addressed at the 2024 DNC.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Gaza is a lingering base-versus-leadership fault line heading into 2028.

insights.claim: Shakir notes the federal minimum wage has been $7.25 since 2007, when a Democratic House and Senate elected in 2006 passed an increase that George W. Bush signed; he argues a Democratic Congress could send a $15-$20 minimum wage or Medicare expansion to Trump, who might claim credit.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Frames a Democratic midterm win as a route to bipartisan-optics populist bills, not only investigations.

insights.claim: Shakir says Medicare for All remains the biggest fight and offers no date, only that it continues as long as Sanders is alive; he says exposure to patient stories radicalizes people toward it.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: No near-term timetable; it stays a messaging anchor.

insights.claim: Minhaj notes approximately 50% of likely voters distrust Democrats on corruption versus 56% distrusting Trump, concluding corruption is normalized and costs Trump less than economic pain.
insights.speaker: Hasan Minhaj
insights.so_what: Corruption is a weak electoral lever relative to pocketbook issues.

insights.claim: Shakir says More Perfect Union, which covers consolidation and structural economics in depth, is now the fastest-growing YouTube channel, which he takes as evidence audiences want depth rather than being treated like fools.
insights.speaker: Faiz Shakir
insights.so_what: Signals an audience for structural economic content in left media.
